app.title: Chromatic
app.subtitle: Space Mission Design
app.intro: Design your own Earth-observation mission by making engineering trade-offs under real-world style constraints.

how: Pick a scientific priority, then choose an orbit, the instruments, the spacecraft systems and a launch vehicle.
Watch mass, cost, power, data and science forecasts update with every choice.
Review the checklist. Blockers must be fixed; warnings are risks you may accept.
Launch, then watch 24 months of operations. Science only counts when data reaches Earth.
Read the debrief to learn how your decisions shaped the result, then try a different design.
menu.title: Chromatic
menu.subtitle: Design. Decide. Discover.

briefing.title: Mission Briefing
briefing.subtitle: Understand the problem, then choose what matters most.
briefing.missionTagline: Monitor environmental change across Earth over a 24-month operation.
briefing.priorityNote: The priority goal multiplies its science. Your target is measured on the weighted total.
briefing.pickFirst: Choose a scientific priority to continue.
briefing.footer: Your priority shapes which instruments and orbits make sense for the whole design.

orbit.title: Orbit Selection
orbit.subtitle: Choose the best orbit profile for your mission goals.
orbit.legendNote: Orbit profiles are didactic simplifications; a sun-synchronous orbit is itself a kind of low Earth orbit.
orbit.footer: Your orbit choice changes science per goal, launch cost, battery needs and which launchers can fly.
orbit.pickFirst: Choose an orbit profile to see its parameters.

payload.title: Payload Design
payload.subtitle: Choose the instruments that will do your science.
payload.scienceHint: Potential, weighted by your priority and orbit
payload.none: No instrument selected yet. Pick at least one.
payload.footer: More instruments mean more science, but also more mass, power, data and cost.
payload.pickFirst: Select at least one instrument to continue.

spacecraft.title: Spacecraft Design
spacecraft.subtitle: Support your instruments with power, communications and a structure.
spacecraft.tipPower: Generation must cover demand. Battery only bridges eclipses; it never fixes a generation deficit.
spacecraft.tipComm: Downlink should be at least the data your instruments produce, or the buffer fills and data is lost.
spacecraft.tipBus: The bus must support payload + power + comms mass. Storage is a buffer, not a transmission speed.
spacecraft.footer: Every subsystem must be balanced for the mission to succeed.
spacecraft.pickFirst: Choose a power system, a communication system and a bus to continue.

launch.title: Launch Planning
launch.subtitle: Pick a launch vehicle that fits your mass, orbit and budget.
launch.footer: Heavier designs need bigger rockets, which cost more. Not every rocket reaches every orbit.
launch.pickFirst: Choose a launch vehicle to continue.

review.title: Mission Review
review.subtitle: Check the design before you commit to launch.
review.warningsNote: Warnings do not block launch, but they can hurt the result.
review.footer: Warnings can hurt the result, blockers cannot be launched.

animation.title: Launch
animation.subtitle: Follow the key moments of your launch.
animation.alt: Animated rocket launching and releasing a satellite above Earth.
animation.footer: This is a simplified, symbolic launch sequence.

simulation.subtitle: Follow your mission in orbit as events unfold.

menu.title: About this game
menu.body: Chromatic is a short strategy game about systems engineering. You design a mission, launch it and learn from the result. Every number is a simplified teaching value.

briefing.title: Why does this matter?
briefing.body: Real missions start from a science question and a budget. Choosing a priority focuses the mission, but it also leaves other goals with less science. There is no single right answer.

orbit.title: Why does this matter?
orbit.body: The orbit decides what the satellite can see, how often, and how long it sits in Earth's shadow. It also changes launch cost and which rockets can reach it.

payload.title: Why does this matter?
payload.body: Instruments create the science, but each one adds mass, power draw and data to carry home. Every extra instrument raises the demands on the rest of the spacecraft.

spacecraft.title: Why does this matter?
spacecraft.body: A spacecraft is a system: power feeds instruments, communications send the data home, and the bus holds everything together. A weak link limits the whole mission.

launch.title: Why does this matter?
launch.body: The launcher sets how much mass you can send and to which orbits. Bigger rockets cost more, so a lighter design can free budget for better instruments.

review.title: Why does this matter?
review.body: Engineers hold design reviews before launch because there is no repair visit later. Blockers are hard limits; warnings are risks that may cost science.

animation.title: Why does this matter?
animation.body: Launch is the moment your plan meets reality. From here on the design is frozen and you can only watch how it performs.

simulation.title: Why does this matter?
simulation.body: Operations are where design choices pay off. Science only counts once data reaches Earth, so power, storage and downlink all matter every month.

debrief.title: Why does this matter?
debrief.body: Missions are judged by results, and teams learn from them. Compare what helped and what hurt, then try another design.

entries.definition: The scientific instruments carried by the satellite.
The structure that holds the satellite together and provides its housekeeping systems. It limits the mass it can support and stores data.
The amount of data the satellite can send to Earth each month.
Onboard memory that holds data until it can be sent. When it is full, new data is lost.
The part of each orbit spent in Earth's shadow, when solar panels make no power and the battery must cover demand.
Generation minus demand. A thin margin leaves little room for degradation.
Total mass the rocket must lift. Each launcher has a maximum.
A low Earth orbit that passes over the same place at the same local time each day, giving consistent lighting.
How long it takes the satellite to observe the same area again.
A simplified chance-of-trouble score. Lower reliability makes negative events more likely in this game.

wildfires.name: Monitor wildfires
wildfires.description: Detect and track wildfires and thermal changes.
wildfires.benefit: Thermal-sensitive instruments earn the most science, and wildfire seasons can add bonus opportunities.
wildfires.tradeoff: Instruments that favor wildfires add less to forests and air quality.

deforestation.name: Detect deforestation
deforestation.description: Follow changes in vegetation and forest cover.
deforestation.benefit: Radar, LiDAR and multispectral imaging all contribute strongly to forest science.
deforestation.tradeoff: The strongest forest instruments are heavy, power hungry and produce a lot of data.

airQuality.name: Analyze atmospheric changes
airQuality.description: Measure atmospheric gases and air quality.
airQuality.benefit: A single spectrometer is cheap and light for the science it delivers.
airQuality.tradeoff: Few instruments see the atmosphere, so you depend on the spectrometer and a good orbit.

leo.name: Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
leo.description: Close to Earth: a balanced, lower-cost profile.
leo.coverage: Good coverage of mid-latitudes with frequent passes.
disadvantages: Forests are viewed at a slightly lower multiplier

sso.name: Sun-synchronous Orbit (SSO)
sso.description: Passes over the same place at the same local time.
advantages: Shortest eclipses, so less battery is needed
disadvantages: Not every launcher can reach it

equatorial.name: Equatorial Orbit
equatorial.coverage: Frequent passes over the tropics, none over the poles.
advantages: Best for tropical wildfires and forests
disadvantages: Longest eclipses and highest battery need

multispectralCamera.name: Multispectral Camera
multispectralCamera.description: Captures data in several wavelengths, helping monitor vegetation, water and land-use change.

thermalSensor.name: Thermal Sensor
thermalSensor.description: Sees heat, making it the best tool for spotting and tracking wildfires.

atmosphericSpectrometer.name: Atmospheric Spectrometer
atmosphericSpectrometer.description: Measures gases in the air. Light, cheap and the key to air-quality science.

sar.name: Synthetic Aperture Radar
sar.description: Sees through clouds and darkness. Powerful for forests, but heavy, hungry and data-heavy.

lidar.name: LiDAR
lidar.description: Laser ranging that measures canopy height. Compact and useful for forest structure.

light.name: Light Bus
light.description: Cheap and light, but supports little mass and stores little data.

standard.name: Standard Bus
standard.description: A balanced structure for mid-size missions.

heavy.name: Heavy Bus
heavy.description: Supports big payloads and stores lots of data, at high cost and mass.

compact.name: Compact Array
compact.description: Small panels and battery. Cheap and light, for low-demand designs.

standard.name: Standard Array
standard.description: Balanced panels and battery for most designs.

large.name: Large Array
large.description: Big panels and battery for power-hungry payloads, at high cost and mass.

endurance.name: Endurance Pack
endurance.description: Modest panels with a big battery, good for long eclipses but not for high demand.

uhf.name: UHF Link
uhf.description: Low-rate, low-power link. Cheap but easily saturated.

xband.name: X-band Link
xband.description: A solid mid-rate link for most payloads.

kaband.name: Ka-band Link
kaband.description: High-rate link for data-heavy instruments, with high power draw and cost.

sparrow.name: Sparrow-1
sparrow.description: Small and cheap. Limited capacity and no sun-synchronous reach.

condor.name: Condor-M
condor.description: A versatile medium launcher that reaches every orbit.

titan.name: Titan-X
titan.description: Heavy and most reliable, but expensive.

solarDegradation.name: Solar degradation
solarDegradation.description: Panels lose efficiency from radiation. Designs with thin power margins suffer most.

instrumentAnomaly.name: Instrument anomaly
instrumentAnomaly.description: A fault temporarily reduces instrument availability.

groundOutage.name: Ground station outage
groundOutage.description: A ground station goes offline, halving the downlink. Tight links suffer most.

solarStorm.name: Solar storm
solarStorm.description: Charged particles reduce power generation and disturb communications.

majorWildfire.name: Major wildfire season
majorWildfire.description: A thermal sensor gets a great chance to observe unusual fires.

deforestationSurge.name: Deforestation surge
deforestationSurge.description: Rapid forest change creates extra opportunity for forest monitoring.

hazeEpisode.name: Haze episode
hazeEpisode.description: A major pollution event gives atmospheric instruments extra opportunity.

clearSkies.name: Clear skies
clearSkies.description: A cloud-free season boosts observation from sun-synchronous orbit.

networkUpgrade.name: Ground network upgrade
networkUpgrade.description: More ground stations temporarily raise downlink capacity.
